input:
A flat carbon steel wall with a thickness of 150 mm separates two process streams. The wall material has a thermal conductivity of 45 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 190 K. Under conditions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, these properties and the temperature difference give a heat flux of 57000 W m-2. This estimate is based only on conduction through the solid wall itself. Surface, or film, resistances at the two sides of the wall are excluded from the calculation. If those resistances were included, the calculated flux would be lower, because the wall-only calculation does not represent the full set of thermal resistances between the process streams. The stated flux should therefore be understood as the result for the specified wall and temperature difference under the stated conduction assumptions, rather than as a complete stream-to-stream heat-transfer result.

It is also important to distinguish heat flux from total heat-transfer rate. The result is expressed for a unit area of wall, and no wall area is specified, so the total rate for a particular installation cannot be obtained from the stated result alone. The calculation further treats conductivity as a property of the wall material over the interval considered and assumes that the temperature varies through the thickness rather than along the faces. Those assumptions are consistent with the simple conduction model used here, but they are not additional measurements. In an actual exchanger or vessel wall, temperature-dependent properties, contact effects, deposits, and surface films may also need to be considered; the present estimate specifically leaves the film resistances outside its scope. The value therefore answers the narrow conduction question posed by the wall data.
target:
A flat carbon steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 45 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across it is 190 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 57000 W m-2.

The result treats the wall as a uniform slab with heat flow normal to its faces. Steady conduction means the temperature profile and flux do not change with time; one-dimensional conduction means lateral temperature differences are neglected. Within those conditions, the stated conductivity, thickness, and temperature difference determine the flux per unit wall area. The calculation is not a complete stream-to-stream heat-transfer calculation. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux. The reported value therefore belongs to the wall resistance alone under the stated temperature difference, and a design calculation for the two streams must add the surface resistances before the flux is used as an overall result.

Heat flux is a rate per unit area, not the total rate through a wall of unspecified area. No area is given, so no total heat-transfer rate follows from the result. The model also treats conductivity as constant for the wall material and the temperature as varying through the thickness, with no lateral variation. Those conditions are the content of the steady one-dimensional assumption. They should not be confused with a measurement of the complete wall assembly. Films at the surfaces belong to a wider calculation that also includes the streams; fouling or contact resistance would belong there as well if they were to be represented. The stated flux remains the wall-only conduction result for the specified slab and temperature difference. Used on that basis, the result can be compared with another wall-only calculation made under the same assumptions and with the same treatment of surface resistance.
